detail.longDescription: I found out that it is possible to check whether certain Numpy result are of a specific Numpy dtype, by checking whether they occur in a list of dtype-class objects: Python 3.11.14 (main, Oct 21 2025, 18:31:21) [GCC 11.2.0] on linux Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information. >>> import numpy as np >>> np.__version__ '2.3.3' >>> np.equal(1,1) in [np.dtypes.BoolDType()] True It seems to indeed perform some check that it is actually the specific dtype: >>> np.equal(1,1) in [np.dtypes.Float32DType()] False I always assumed that the in operator, aka the __contains__ method, was equivalent to just looping over the list and checking each element for equality. What's a bit bizarre here is that np.equal(1,1) should rather be an instance of BoolDType , whereas the in check appears to look whether it occurs as a value in the list. Indeed, none of the usual checks work when directly comparing with the element of that list: >>> np.equal(1,1) == np.dtypes.BoolDType() False >>> np.equal(1,1) is np.dtypes.BoolDType() False >>> isinstance(np.equal(1,1), np.dtypes.BoolDType()) Traceback (most recent call last): File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module> TypeError: isinstance() arg 2 must be a type, a tuple of types, or a union isinstance does work for the class of BoolDType , i.e. by not generating an instance of it, but then the comparisons just yield False : >>> isinstance(np.equal(1,1), np.dtypes.BoolDType) False >>> np.equal(1,1) == np.dtypes.BoolDType False >>> np.equal(1,1) is np.dtypes.BoolDType False How does the in list check actually give a sensible behaviour here? How can this behaviour be achieved without querying a list? I'm interested in the behaviour for this Numpy-specific use, but would prefer to understand the general principle
